title: Beyond the Red Carpet: Indian Cinema Had Its Quietest — and Most Important — Year at Cannes.
excerpt: While Aishwarya and Kangana dominated headlines, a student film made official selection from 2,750 entries, a short film screened at Marché du Film, and South Asian storytelling got its first-ever main stage panel.
body:
The 79th Cannes Film Festival ended on May 23. If you followed the Indian coverage, you saw sarees, couture, and a debate about whether Kangana Ranaut was defending or trolling Aishwarya Rai Bachchan. You saw selfies. You saw outfit changes.

What you probably did not see is what Indian cinema actually accomplished at Cannes this year. And for the first time in several editions, what happened off the red carpet may matter more than what happened on it.

## 'Shadows of the Moonless Nights' — One of Two Indian Films in Official Selection

Out of 2,750 submissions from around the world, the Cannes selection committee chose a handful for the prestigious La Cinef section — the festival's competition for film school works. Among them was Shadows of the Moonless Nights, directed by Mehar Malhotra and featuring actor Prayrak Mehta and actor-casting director Nikita Grover.

The selection is significant not because it guarantees a career — though La Cinef alumni include some of today's most celebrated arthouse directors — but because it signals what kind of Indian storytelling the international festival circuit is looking for. It is not the mythological spectacles or the franchise action films that dominate domestic box offices. It is intimate, formally adventurous work that speaks in a cinematic language Cannes recognizes.

For young Indian filmmakers, particularly those studying abroad or working outside the Bollywood ecosystem, this is a validation that matters.

## Ahsaas Channa's 'Gudgudi' at Marché du Film

Ahsaas Channa — known to Indian audiences from Kota Factory and other streaming hits — screened her short film Gudgudi at the Marché du Film, Cannes' parallel market section where buyers, distributors, and industry professionals discover new work.

Channa has spoken about the significance of having Indian narratives represented at Cannes beyond the celebrity presence. Gudgudi was featured alongside works from established and emerging filmmakers, and its screening represents a broader trend: Indian actors moving behind the camera and finding international platforms for work that would struggle to get theatrical distribution at home.

## The First-Ever South Asian Panel on the Main Stage

Perhaps the most structurally important development at Cannes 2026 was Tasveer's panel — the first and only official South Asian panel on the main stage at the Cannes Marché du Film.

Tasveer, a platform focused on South Asian visual storytelling, brought together voices from entertainment, technology, audience analytics, and independent filmmaking. The panel's subject was the future of globally scalable South Asian storytelling — not whether Indian films can make money overseas (they obviously can), but whether the kind of stories being told can travel beyond the diaspora audience that already shows up for them.

This is the question that separates Indian cinema's current international moment from a genuine structural breakthrough. The domestic industry produces over 1,500 films a year. A handful cross over — usually through the action-spectacle route (RRR, KGF) or the prestige-festival route (All We Imagine as Light). The gap between those two pathways is enormous, and Tasveer's panel attempted to map the territory in between.

## What the Diaspora Should Notice

For NRIs who care about Indian cinema's global standing, Cannes 2026 offers a mixed signal.

On one hand, the celebrity presence continues to grow. Indian stars are now fixtures at Cannes, not curiosities. L'Oréal, Gucci, and Schiaparelli compete for Indian faces on the Croisette. That visibility has value — it normalizes Indian participation at the highest levels of global culture.

On the other hand, India's representation in the actual film competition remains minimal. No Indian feature film competed for the Palme d'Or this year. No Indian film was in Un Certain Regard. The student film and the short film are promising, but they are entry points, not arrivals.

The Palme d'Or went to Fjord, continuing a streak of European and East Asian dominance at the top of the festival. Peter Jackson and Barbra Streisand received Honorary Palmes d'Or. Five female directors were in competition — a record — but none were Indian.

## The Long Game

Payal Kapadia's All We Imagine as Light won the Grand Prix at Cannes in 2024. That victory was supposed to open a door. Two years later, the door is open, but the corridor behind it is longer than anyone expected.

Indian cinema's Cannes story is no longer about whether it belongs. That debate is settled. The question now is what kind of presence India builds — one defined by red carpet moments and brand partnerships, or one defined by films that compete for and win the festival's highest honours.

The student film from 2,750 entries. The short film at the market. The first South Asian panel on the main stage. These are not headlines. They are foundations. Whether anyone builds on them depends on what happens between now and Cannes 2027.
